additional_information: This course examines gender roles and gender relations using ethnographic examples from a range of different cultures. Drawing on feminist and gender theories we approach gender as something that is actively enacted and explore how it intersects with factors like class, age, and ethnicity. More specifically we will apply a gendered perspective to analyzing issues such as childhood socialization, division of labour, sexuality and the body, religion, international development and migration. While the emphasis is on cultural aspects, biological factors will also be addressed.

course_name: EXPLORING BIO-ANTHROPOLOGY: Crime Scene Investigation and Forensic Anthropology Practices
additional_information: This course provides an in-depth exploration of crime scene investigation techniques and their intersection with forensic anthropology. Students will learn the fundamental principles of forensic anthropology and how they apply to crime scene recovery, documentation, analysis of human remains, and personal identification. Emphasis will be placed on the ethical treatment of human remains in a medicolegal context, evidence handling, scene mapping, and legal considerations in forensic contexts. A core objective is to expose students to real-world forensic applications through guest lectures from professionals in forensic investigation. These lectures will help bridge the gap between theoretical knowledge and practical forensic casework, demonstrating the interdisciplinary nature of forensic anthropology. Students will cultivate critical thinking, problem-solving, and deductive reasoning skills while gaining expertise in medical and legal terminology essential for effective communication in forensic contexts. They will work independently to enhance their analytical and interpretive abilities, developing the competence to assess challenges and formulate solutions in forensic investigations.

additional_information: Explores links between the languages, cultures and social systems of the Mayan-speaking peoples of Mexico and Guatemala, from precolonial times to the present. Examines issues of worldview, identity, religion and power through engagement with a variety of sources. These sources include pre-Hispanic Maya texts, Colonial Period narratives like the Popol Vuh, and contemporary ethnographies. No prior familiarity with Maya languages or cultures is assumed.

subject: ANTH
course_name: CULTURAL ANTHROPOLOGY: Bread Beyond Borders: Food and Migration
additional_information: After an introduction to key course concepts, this course will use food as evidence, tool and lens to address how migrants live out their daily lives in their new homes. Namely, we will explore how food plays a role in migrants' identity negotiations and presentation, in their efforts to maintain connection to their homeland and in their building of new homes in their migrant locations. Using popular culture, cookbooks and stories from migrants themselves, we will explore how bread is beyond borders.

subject: ANTH
course_name: BIOLOGICAL ANTHROPOLOGY: Exploring Diversity in Healthcare
additional_information: This course explores the intersection of human diversity and healthcare, focusing on how biological, social, and cultural differences influence health outcomes. Through a problem-based learning approach, students investigate contemporary issues related to race, gender, and other social categories, with an emphasis on understanding when and how diversity should be integrated into healthcare delivery and policy. Students will critically analyze how healthcare systems either accommodate or marginalize diverse populations and will develop evidence-based strategies to promote inclusive, equitable care.

subject: ANTH
course_name: METHOD AND THEORY: Applied Archaeological Sciences for Reconstructing the Human Past
additional_information: How do archaeologists employ scientific methods to reconstruct dynamic past worlds? This upper-level course examines the theoretical and methodological foundations of applied archaeological science, emphasizing how biological, chemical, and physical analyses are used to interpret ancient environments and human activities. Students will explore how techniques such as stable isotope analysis, ancient DNA and proteomics, archaeobotany, and zooarchaeology illuminate patterns of subsistence, mobility, landscape use, and ecological transformation. Drawing on case studies from around the world and hands-on exercises, the course situates these archaeological sciences within broader anthropological and theoretical frameworks, including posthumanist studies and collaborative approaches to archaeological research. Attention will be given to the biological and ecological dimensions of the archaeological record, while emphasizing how scientific evidence contributes to holistic reconstructions of past human–environmental systems through the integration of diverse archaeological proxies Students will gain a critical and practical understanding of how these archaeological dataset are generated, analyzed, and synthesized to build robust interpretations of the past.

course_name: SPECIAL STUDIES: Curatorial Direction: Curating Indigenous Art
additional_information: In this course students will study the history and theory of contemporary Indigenous art exhibitions and curatorial practice, focusing on emerging work produced in Canada and comparative international contexts. In this course you will learn about the work of contemporary Indigenous curators and artists; study key texts, concepts, interventions and innovations in the display and dissemination of Indigenous art; and draw on case studies from significant exhibitions, biennials, and public art events over the last thirty years in order to create your own imagined exhibitions. We will examine current issues, themes and frames such as Indigeneity, diaspora, sovereignty, self-determination, resistance, and resurgence. We will cultivate an understanding of the legacies and ongoing impacts of settler colonialism on Indigenous peoples and consider how this continues to influence gallery and museum practices, arts education, and public space and place, with a focus on how Indigenous curators and artists challenge, intervene, and disrupt these histories, institutions, sites, and the spaces between them. Students will gain an understanding of the Indigenous arts milieu through weekly readings, museum and gallery tours (possibly virtual), and by guest lecturers from across the fields and disciplines of contemporary Indigenous art and curatorial practice. Taking a hands-on approach, students will bring together theory and practice as they propose and plan an exhibition of Indigenous arts from concept and proposal, to (imagined) installation and catalogue creation.

additional_information: This advanced fourth-year course offers an in-depth examination of the dynamic entrepreneurial landscape and intricate ecosystems that support Indigenous business development in Canada. It is designed for students seeking to understand the unique opportunities, challenges, and support structures available to Indigenous entrepreneurs. Open to non-business students via request for registration starting on August 1. https://www.uvic.ca/gustavson/undergraduate/minor/index.php

subject: COM
course_name: ADVANCED MANAGEMENT TOPICS: Business and Human Rights
additional_information: This course provides an overview of the field of business and human rights (BHR). We will focus on key aspects and challenges human rights pose to the work of organizations and how they can engage with those issues to atone and remedy past transgressions, assess and avoid causing harm, and establish parameters and mechanisms to prevent future violations. Classes will cover topics such as ethics, violations, responsibilities, UN principles, discrimination, racism, slavery, climate change, and Indigenous peoples. Open to non-business students via request for registration starting on August 1. https://www.uvic.ca/gustavson/undergraduate/minor/index.php

subject: COM
course_name: ADVANCED MANAGEMENT TOPICS: Pursuing Happiness and Career Success at Work
additional_information: This course will help students understand the core elements of happiness and practical strategies for how to pursue these elements at work.  The course will also focus on the seven elements of career success that cut across industries, cultures, jobs and careers while assessing their importance to each student and identifying individual strengths and strategies for pursuing success at work in the changing landscape of the Fourth Industrial Revolution which entails not only getting the most out of technology like A.I. but also out of each individual. Open to non-business students via request for registration starting on August. https://www.uvic.ca/gustavson/undergraduate/minor/index.php

subject: COM
course_name: ADVANCED MANAGEMENT TOPICS: Deglobalization in an Age of Autocracy
additional_information: This course will explore the social, political and economic determinants and consequences of deglobalization. The evolving context for business will be highlighted, including greater uncertainty, increasing politicization and supply chain disruptions that stem from the weakening of multilateral agreements, threats to a rules-based world order and the erosion of democratic institutions.

subject: CS
course_name: TOPICS IN CANADIAN STUDIES: How to Change the World: Canadian Grassroots Organizations
additional_information: Grassroots community organizations are at the heart of much social, environmental and economic change in Canada. They have historically been the “small groups of committed citizens” that “change the world” for the better. This course explores the history, achievements and possibilities inherent in grassroots organizations in Canada, using provocative examples from across the country but with a focus on British Columbia movements. The course will also include a community-engaged component, offering opportunity for students to engage with a local community organization, pairing their class learning on the theory, practice and history of grassroots social and environmental justice movements with on-the-ground experience.

additional_information: Topic description: this seminar course explores the major pressing topics in Canadian mammal conservation and the ecological theories around species declines and recoveries. Students will get exposed to a comprehensive survey of Canadian mammal species, their conservation status, and the ecological problems facing species at risk. course_name: SPECIAL TOPICS CLINICAL PSYCH: Climate Anxiety and Grief
additional_information: This course explores recent epidemiological data linking climate anxiety and grief to adverse mental health outcomes across the globe. We survey research from multiple academic disciplines demonstrating the adverse impacts of climate anxiety/grief on human emotions, cognitions, behaviours and systems. We connect experientially with our own climate distress and practice interventions designed to restore our courage and our sense of purpose for climate engagement.

subject: PSYC
course_name: ADV SPCL TPCS:PSYC: Psychology for Instruction
additional_information: Psychological science has much to contribute to enhancing teaching and learning across a range of educational contexts. Drawing on contemporary research, this course will explore evidenced-based principles from psychology that inform the design of effective and responsive learning environments. The course will be of interest to students who are interested in (a) applying psychological science to instructional design or assessment, (b) developing instructional tools and interventions, (c ) pursuing careers related to education or instructional design, or (d) contributing to research in the psychology of education. This is a good course for future teaching assistants.
